### dangerous-action

This rules warn the user if a dangerous action is used. It's mainly focused on untrusted artifacts.

It is common practice to use artifacts to pass data between different workflows. We often encounter this with the `workflow_run` trigger where the triggering workflow will prepare some data that will then be sent to the triggered workflow. Given the untrusted nature of this artifact data, it is crucial to treat it with caution and recognize it as a potential threat. The vulnerability arises from the fact that external entities, such as malicious actors, can influence the content of the artifact data.

### dangerous-write

GitHub will create default environment variables that can be used inside every step in a workflow. The `GITHUB_ENV` and `GITHUB_OUTPUT` variables are particularly interesting. It is possible to define environment variable in a step and to use this variable in another one. This can be done by writing it to the associated variable variable. If a user can control the content of the variable that is being set it can lead to arbitrary code execution.

36	type RuleDangerousCheckout struct {
37		actionlint.RuleBase
38		filterTriggers []string

40		// envTaint tracks, for the job currently being visited, which environment variable

42		// branch. It's rebuilt from scratch for every job, since env var scope doesn't cross
43		// job boundaries.

50	func NewRuleDangerousCheckout(filterTriggers []string) *RuleDangerousCheckout {
51		return &RuleDangerousCheckout{
52			RuleBase: actionlint.NewRuleBase(

62		// check on event and set skip if needed

69	func (rule *RuleDangerousCheckout) VisitJobPre(n *actionlint.Job) error {
70		// env vars and step outputs are scoped to the job they are defined in: reset the
71		// taint tracking state for every job instead of leaking it across jobs.

82	
83		if rule.skip {
84			return nil
85		}
86	
87		switch e := n.Exec.(type) {
88		case *actionlint.ExecRun:
89			rule.checkManualCheckout(e)

98	func (rule *RuleDangerousCheckout) checkCheckoutAction(action *actionlint.ExecAction) {
99		if action.Uses.ContainsExpression() {
100			// Cannot parse specification made with interpolation. Give up
101			return
102		}
103	
104		spec := action.Uses.Value
105	
106		// search for checkout action
107		if strings.HasPrefix(spec, "actions/checkout") {
108			ref := action.Inputs["ref"]
109	
110			if ref != nil && rule.isValueUntrusted(ref.Value.Value) {
111				rule.Errorf(
112					ref.Value.Pos,
113					"Use of 'actions/checkout' with a custom ref that can be controlled by the pull request's head branch.",

120	// value assigned to an env var / step output) is derived from the pull request's head
121	// branch. See the judgment boundary documented above the RuleDangerousCheckout type.
122	func (rule *RuleDangerousCheckout) isValueUntrusted(raw string) bool {
123		if !containsExpression(raw) {
124			// hardcoded value (branch name, full ref, sha, ...): never attacker controlled.
125			return false
126		}
127	
128		for _, expr := range extractExpressions(raw) {
129			untrusted, recognized := rule.classifyExpr(expr)
130			if !recognized || untrusted {
131				return true
132			}
133		}
134	
135		return false
136	}

138	// classifyExpr inspects the content of a single "${{ ... }}" expression. recognized
139	// reports whether the expression matched one of the known source patterns (pull
140	// request base/head, env context, step outputs context); untrusted is only meaningful
141	// when recognized is true.
142	func (rule *RuleDangerousCheckout) classifyExpr(expr string) (untrusted bool, recognized bool) {
143		switch {
144		case common.TrustedPullRequestBaseRegexp.MatchString(expr):
145			return false, true
146	
147		case common.UntrustedPullRequestHeadRegexp.MatchString(expr):
148			return true, true
149	
150		case common.EnvContextRegexp.MatchString(expr):
151			m := common.EnvContextRegexp.FindStringSubmatch(expr)
152	
153			return rule.envTaint[m[1]], true
154	
155		case common.StepOutputContextRegexp.MatchString(expr):
156			m := common.StepOutputContextRegexp.FindStringSubmatch(expr)
157	
158			return rule.outputTaint[m[1]+"/"+m[2]], true
159	
160		default:
161			return false, false
162		}
163	}

166	// from VisitJobPre), whether its value is untrusted.
167	func (rule *RuleDangerousCheckout) collectEnvTaint(env *actionlint.Env) {
168		if env == nil || env.Vars == nil {
169			return
170		}
171	
172		for _, v := range env.Vars {
173			rule.envTaint[v.Name.Value] = rule.isValueUntrusted(v.Value.Value)
174		}
175	}

179	// "env.NAME" or "steps.<id>.outputs.NAME" can be traced back to this assignment.
180	func (rule *RuleDangerousCheckout) collectRunTaint(step *actionlint.Step, exec *actionlint.ExecRun) {
181		script := exec.Run.Value

183		for _, m := range common.GitHubEnvAssignRegexp.FindAllStringSubmatch(script, -1) {

192			rule.outputTaint[step.ID.Value+"/"+m[1]] = rule.isShellValueUntrusted(m[2])

# https://github.com/synacktiv/octoscan (poisoned pipeline execution via
# "pull_request_target" + a custom "actions/checkout" ref).

# The other three jobs use refs that cannot be influenced by a fork pull request and
# must not be reported (they would all have been false positives with the previous,
# purely syntactic "is this ref a plain branch name" check).
#
name: poisoned-pipeline-sample

on:
  pull_request_target

jobs:
  # TRUE POSITIVE: the head sha is captured into an env var in one step, then used as
  # the checkout ref in a later step. The value is attacker controlled whenever the pull
  # request comes from a fork, so this must still be reported even though "ref:" itself
  # never mentions "head" textually.
  build-fork-controlled-ref:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - name: capture untrusted head sha
        run: |
          echo "TARGET_REF=${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha }}" >> "$GITHUB_ENV"

      - name: checkout attacker-controlled ref
        uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with:
          ref: ${{ env.TARGET_REF }}

  # SAFE: hardcoded, protected branch. No expression at all, so it can't be influenced
  # by the pull request.

    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

      - name: checkout main

  # never to the fork that opened the pull request.

### dangerous-checkout

Triggers like `workflow_run` or `pull_request_target` run in a privileged context, as they have read access to secrets and potentially have write access on the targeted repository. Performing an explicit checkout on the untrusted code will result in the attacker code being downloaded in such context.

![excalidraw](img/excalidraw.png)

#### judgment boundary for `actions/checkout`'s `ref:`

- A `ref:` with no `${{ ... }}` expression (a plain branch name, a full `refs/heads/...` path, a hardcoded sha) is chosen by the workflow author and is never flagged, regardless of its shape.
- `github.event.pull_request.base.*` and `github.base_ref` always describe the base (target) repository, controlled by the maintainers. They are never flagged, even on `pull_request_target`.
- `github.event.pull_request.head.*` and `github.head_ref` describe the pull request's head (source) branch. When the PR comes from a fork (`head.repo.fork == true`), this is attacker controlled; since that boolean can't be evaluated statically, any use of `head.*` is always flagged.
- `env.NAME` and `steps.<id>.outputs.<name>` are resolved by tracing, within the same job, how `NAME`/the output was last assigned: a job-level `env:`, or a `$GITHUB_ENV`/`$GITHUB_OUTPUT` write in an earlier step's `run:` script. The ref is flagged only if that assignment is itself derived from `head.*` (directly, or transitively through another tainted env var/output); it's not flagged if the assignment is provably safe (hardcoded value, or derived from `base.*`).
- Any other dynamic expression that doesn't match the patterns above (an unrelated input, a secret, an untraced step output, ...) keeps the rule's original conservative behavior and is flagged, since it can't be proven safe.

See `core/rules/rule_dangerous_checkout.go` and `core/rules/rule_dangerous_checkout_test.go` for the implementation and test cases, and `core/rules/testdata/poisoned_pipeline_sample.yml` for an example workflow mixing a truly fork-controllable indirect ref with refs that must not be reported.

go.mod/go.sum untouched, only the intended files changed. Everything is in order:

**Changes:**
- `core/rules/rule_dangerous_checkout.go`: replaced the blunt "any non-literal ref is dangerous" regex with a classifier that treats hardcoded refs and `pull_request.base.*`/`github.base_ref` as safe, flags `pull_request.head.*`/`github.head_ref` as unsafe, and traces `env.NAME`/`steps.<id>.outputs.<name>` back through job-level `env:` and `$GITHUB_ENV`/`$GITHUB_OUTPUT` writes in prior steps within the same job — falling back to the old conservative "flag if unrecognized" behavior for anything it can't classify.
- `common/helpers.go`: added new regexes for this classification (`UntrustedPullRequestHeadRegexp`, `TrustedPullRequestBaseRegexp`, `EnvContextRegexp`, `StepOutputContextRegexp`, `GitHubEnvAssignRegexp`, `GitHubOutputAssignRegexp`, `ShellVarRefRegexp`) — purely additive, existing vars/behavior untouched.
- `core/rules/helpers.go`: added `extractExpressions` helper — additive only.
- `core/rules/rule_dangerous_checkout_test.go`: 12 new tests covering direct dangerous refs, indirect env/step-output taint propagation (both dangerous and safe chains), protected-branch/base-sha false-positive fixes, manual-checkout regression guard, and the unrecognized-expression conservative default.
- `core/rules/testdata/poisoned_pipeline_sample.yml` (+ `.scan.log`): sample workflow with one real PPE-exploitable job and three safe jobs that would previously have been false positives.
- `README.md`: documented the new judgment boundary under `dangerous-checkout`.

**Verification:** `go build ./...`, `go vet ./...`, and `go test ./... -run DangerousCheckout -v` all pass (12/12). `go run . scan ./core/rules/testdata/poisoned_pipeline_sample.yml` confirms only the fork-controllable indirect ref is flagged by `[dangerous-checkout]`; the hardcoded-branch, base-sha, and indirect-base-ref jobs are not. Note: the task's literal `go run octoscan.go scan ...` fails with `undefined: versionString` on the pristine upstream snapshot too (verified via `git stash`) — `go run` with a single filename doesn't pull in sibling `version.go` in the `main` package. This is pre-existing and unrelated to the fix; `go run . scan ...` is the working equivalent, and both outputs are saved in `core/rules/testdata/poisoned_pipeline_sample.scan.log`.
